title: The register grows teeth
subtitle: ECCTA 2023, identity verification and failure to prevent fraud
objectives: Explain the three pillars of the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023: identity verification, Companies House's enhanced powers, and the failure to prevent fraud offence
State the elements of the failure to prevent fraud offence and identify which organisations it applies to
Compare the failure to prevent fraud offence to the Bribery Act 2010 s 7 template it is modelled on, and identify why its practical application is still largely untested

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This is the most recently commenced law in the whole module, and it changes what 'checking a company's filings' actually means. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You know the headline reforms — this lesson checks whether you can place each one on its actual timeline.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. Expect questions that test exact commencement and transition dates, since this is a knowledge-led lesson built around a moving timeline.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and hold the three pillars — identity verification, Companies House's powers, and failure to prevent fraud — as three separate reforms. They're often blurred together, and this lesson's whole structure depends on keeping them apart.

overview.hook: For as long as companies have existed on the UK register, anyone could be appointed a director using nothing more than a name and a date of birth — no proof either belonged to a real, verified person. The Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 ends that. This lesson covers the single biggest shift in company law administration in a generation: a register that checks who you are, a regulator that can now say no, and a new corporate offence built to catch companies that let fraud happen on their watch.
overview.lawStatedNotice: This lesson covers the single biggest moving target in the whole module. Companies House identity verification is rolling out in phases from 18 November 2025, and existing directors and PSCs have a transition window running into late 2026 — the exact final deadline should be checked against current gov.uk/Companies House guidance rather than assumed from this lesson alone. The 'failure to prevent fraud' offence has been in force since 1 September 2025 but has no reported case law behind it yet, so its practical scope rests on statutory text and official guidance, not judicial interpretation. Law stated as at 23 September 2026.

parts.heading: Three reforms, one Act: the shape of ECCTA 2023
parts.voice: structural — a map students will return to across the rest of the lesson
body: The Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 (ECCTA) is a large, mixed statute, but for this lesson it breaks into three genuinely distinct reforms, each with its own commencement date and its own logic. Confusing them is the single most common error students make in this area, so treat this part as the checklist the rest of the lesson hangs off.

First, identity verification: Companies House moves from a register that simply records whatever names and details it is given, to one that checks a person actually exists and is who they claim to be, before letting them act as a director, a person with significant control (PSC), or a filer on the register at all. Second, enhanced powers for Companies House itself: for the first time, the registrar can query, reject and remove information, rather than acting as a passive filing repository. Third, and separately again, a new corporate criminal offence — failure to prevent fraud — aimed at large organisations that let fraud happen within their business without adequate prevention procedures in place.

None of these three reforms depends on the others for its own legal force, and each commenced on its own timetable. Keep that structure in mind: an exam question testing 'what changed under ECCTA' is really asking you to identify which of the three pillars is actually in play on the facts given.

components.term: Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 (ECCTA)
components.definition: The statute introducing mandatory identity verification for company officers and filers, expanded investigative and enforcement powers for Companies House, and the new 'failure to prevent fraud' corporate offence — three separate reforms with separate commencement dates, unified by a single aim of making UK companies harder to use as vehicles for economic crime.

interaction.prompt: Name the three separate reforms ECCTA 2023 introduces that this lesson covers.
acceptableAnswers: identity verification, enhanced Companies House powers, failure to prevent fraud offence
mandatory ID checks, registrar powers, failure to prevent fraud
interaction.modelAnswer: Mandatory identity verification for directors, PSCs and filers; enhanced powers for Companies House to query, reject and remove register information; and the new 'failure to prevent fraud' corporate offence.

parts.heading: Identity verification: who, and by when
parts.voice: cautious — precise about dates, explicit about what remains unsettled
body: Part 1 of ECCTA requires identity verification (IDV) for anyone acting as a director of a UK company, anyone registered as a person with significant control, and anyone who files documents at Companies House on a company's behalf — either directly, or through an Authorised Corporate Service Provider (ACSP) acting as an agent, who must themselves be registered and carry out the checks.

The rollout is phased rather than a single switch-flip. Companies House confirmed identity verification began rolling out from 18 November 2025, starting with new director appointments and new incorporations, where verification is now a precondition of a valid appointment or filing. For the much larger population of existing directors and PSCs already on the register before that date, the Act allows a transition window, rather than requiring immediate retrospective verification of everyone overnight — a transition window that, as at this lesson's date, is understood to run into late 2026, though the precise final deadline for existing office-holders should always be checked against current gov.uk and Companies House guidance rather than treated as fixed by this lesson.

The consequence of missing the deadline, once it fully applies, is significant: an unverified person cannot be validly appointed or continue validly acting as a director or PSC, and filings made without proper verification can be rejected outright — which is the direct link to the enhanced registrar powers covered in Part 3.

components.label: Who must verify, and the phasing
points: Directors — verification required for new appointments from 18 November 2025; existing directors given a transition window running into late 2026 (check current guidance for the exact date)
Persons with significant control (PSCs) — same phased approach as directors
Filers — anyone filing on a company's behalf, either directly or via a registered Authorised Corporate Service Provider (ACSP)
Consequence of non-verification once the relevant deadline passes: invalid appointment, and filings liable to rejection

interaction.prompt: Put these identity verification milestones in the order they occur under the phased rollout.
items: Identity verification begins rolling out for new director appointments and incorporations (18 November 2025)
Existing directors and PSCs verify within the transition window running into late 2026
Unverified existing office-holders face invalid appointment status and filing rejection once the deadline passes
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the sequence: the Act's passage comes first, then a phased start for new appointments, then a transition period for the existing population, and only then real consequences for anyone who hasn't verified by the time that window closes.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — Royal Assent comes before any rollout; new appointments and incorporations were the first group brought into scope (from 18 November 2025); existing directors and PSCs get a transition window after that; the practical bite (invalid appointment, rejected filings) only follows once that window has run its course.

parts.heading: A registrar that can finally say no
parts.voice: direct — contrasts the old and new roles of Companies House
body: Before ECCTA, Companies House operated on a largely 'file and forget' basis: it was legally required to accept documents that met the formal filing requirements, without any general power to question whether the content was accurate, consistent, or even plausible. That gap was well known and frequently exploited — companies could be registered with obviously fictitious officers, addresses that didn't exist, or accounts that made no internal sense, and the registrar had almost no tools to intervene.

ECCTA changes that role fundamentally. The registrar now has an explicit statutory objective to ensure information on the register is accurate and to prevent the register being used for unlawful purposes, backed by real powers: to query information provided and require further evidence or explanation before accepting a filing; to reject filings that appear inconsistent, incomplete, or fraudulent; and to remove or annotate information already on the register that appears to be false, whether historic or newly filed. Companies House also gained stronger gateways to share data proactively with law enforcement and other regulators, rather than waiting to be asked.

This is the pillar most likely to interact with identity verification on the facts of a problem question: a filing submitted by an unverified person, or containing details inconsistent with verified identity records, is exactly the kind of submission the registrar's new query-and-reject powers are designed to catch.

components.citation: Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023, Part 1 (illustrative summary of the registrar's new functions)
components.text: The registrar's objectives, in exercising functions under the Companies Acts, include ensuring that information on the register is accurate and that the register is a reliable and complete source of information, and preventing companies and other persons from carrying out unlawful activities, or facilitating the carrying out by others of unlawful activities. The registrar may query information delivered to it, require further evidence, and reject or remove filings that do not meet these objectives.
elements: Statutory objective: accuracy and reliability of the register
Statutory objective: preventing companies being used for unlawful purposes
New power to query and demand further evidence before accepting a filing
New power to reject or remove inaccurate or fraudulent information

interaction.prompt: Under the registrar's new statutory objectives, what changed most fundamentally about the registrar's role compared with the pre-ECCTA position?
options: A shift from passively accepting formally compliant filings to actively verifying accuracy and querying suspicious submissions
The registrar became a criminal prosecuting authority in place of the Crown Prosecution Service
The registrar lost the power to accept any company filings at all
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The core change is the shift from a purely administrative, formally-compliant filing role to an active gatekeeping one, with real power to question and reject.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite. The registrar remains the body that accepts company filings and is not a prosecuting authority — the real change is the shift from passive acceptance of formally compliant documents to active querying, rejection and removal powers aimed at accuracy.

parts.heading: Failure to prevent fraud: a new corporate offence
parts.voice: statute-first — builds the offence from its elements
body: Section 199 and Schedule 12 create the third pillar, and the one that most directly exposes large organisations to criminal liability rather than administrative consequences. The offence is committed where a person associated with a 'relevant body' — an employee, agent, subsidiary, or anyone else performing services for or on behalf of the organisation — commits a specified fraud offence intending to benefit the organisation (or, in some circumstances, a person to whom the associated person provides services on the organisation's behalf), and the organisation did not have reasonable fraud prevention procedures in place.

The offence only applies to 'large organisations' — those meeting at least two of three thresholds: annual turnover above £36 million, balance sheet total above £18 million, or more than 250 employees. A small or medium-sized company, whatever fraud its staff commit, falls outside the offence entirely, though its staff and any complicit directors remain separately liable under ordinary fraud law.

The organisation's only defence is to show it had reasonable fraud prevention procedures in place at the time of the offence, or that it was reasonable, in the circumstances, not to have any such procedures at all. Like the Bribery Act 2010 model this is built on, official guidance sets out the kind of procedures — risk assessment, proportionate policies, top-level commitment, due diligence, training and monitoring — that are likely to be treated as reasonable, without any single checklist guaranteeing the defence in every case.

components.citation: Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023, s 199 and Sch 12 (summary of the offence)
components.text: A relevant body is guilty of an offence if a person associated with it commits a fraud offence specified in Schedule 12, intending to benefit (directly or indirectly) the relevant body or a person to whom the associated person provides services on the relevant body's behalf. It is a defence for the relevant body to show that, at the time the fraud offence was committed, it had in place such prevention procedures as it was reasonable in all the circumstances to expect, or that it was not reasonable in the circumstances to expect it to have any prevention procedures in place.
elements: An 'associated person' commits a specified fraud offence
Intention to benefit the relevant body (or its client, via the associated person's services)
The relevant body is a 'large organisation' (two of: turnover >£36m, balance sheet >£18m, >250 employees)
Defence: reasonable fraud prevention procedures were in place, or reasonable not to have any

interaction.prompt: Which scenario is capable of triggering the failure to prevent fraud offence?
interaction.scenarioA: A small logistics company with 40 employees and modest turnover discovers a junior employee has been falsifying delivery invoices to inflate the company's reported revenue.
interaction.scenarioB: A large listed manufacturer, meeting the size thresholds, discovers a regional sales manager has been falsifying customer contracts to inflate reported sales figures and boost the division's, and the company's, reported performance.
interaction.explanation: B involves a 'large organisation' under the two-of-three thresholds, an associated person (the sales manager) committing a fraud offence intending to benefit the company through inflated performance figures — the fact pattern the offence targets. A falls outside the offence entirely because the company is not large enough, whatever the underlying conduct; the employee, and potentially the company under ordinary principles, may still face other liability, but not this offence.

parts.heading: The Bribery Act template, and the case law gap
parts.voice: reflective — closes by placing the new offence in its proper comparative and evidential context
body: The failure to prevent fraud offence was deliberately drafted on the model Parliament had already used once before: Bribery Act 2010, s 7, the offence of a commercial organisation failing to prevent bribery by a person associated with it, subject to an 'adequate procedures' defence. Both offences share the same basic architecture — liability attaches to the organisation for an associated person's underlying wrongdoing, without needing to prove any individual director or 'directing mind' personally authorised or even knew about it, and the organisation's only escape route is showing its prevention systems were good enough.

That architecture is a deliberate departure from the older 'identification doctrine' that otherwise governs most corporate criminal liability in England and Wales, under which a company is only guilty if a sufficiently senior individual — someone whose acts and state of mind count as the company's own — personally has the necessary guilty mind. Failure-to-prevent offences sidestep that difficulty entirely: they don't need a guilty senior mind at all, only an associated person's underlying offence and inadequate prevention systems. (ECCTA separately reforms the identification doctrine itself, for other economic crime offences, under s 198 — a related but distinct reform, worth knowing exists but outside this lesson's scope.)

One honest limitation belongs at the centre of this lesson, not its footnotes: because the failure to prevent fraud offence only came into force on 1 September 2025, there is no reported case law yet testing what 'reasonable fraud prevention procedures' actually requires in practice, in the way well over a decade of Bribery Act enforcement and guidance has shaped 'adequate procedures' under s 7. Treat the Bribery Act comparison as the best available guide to how courts are likely to approach the new offence, not as a guarantee of how they will.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often assume the failure to prevent fraud offence requires proving a director or senior manager knew about or authorised the fraud, just as under the older identification doctrine.
components.whyItsWrong: That's precisely what the 'failure to prevent' model is designed to avoid. Liability turns on the associated person's underlying fraud offence plus inadequate prevention procedures at the organisational level — no proof of a director's personal knowledge or authorisation is required, which is exactly why this model is considered a significant expansion of corporate criminal exposure compared with the identification doctrine.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that there is a well-developed body of UK case law interpreting 'reasonable fraud prevention procedures' under the failure to prevent fraud offence?
interaction.explanation: There is no reported case law yet. The offence only came into force on 1 September 2025. The Bribery Act 2010 s 7 comparison and official guidance are the best available indicators of how 'reasonable procedures' is likely to be assessed, but courts have not yet tested the new offence's boundaries.

testPool.prompt: Which Act introduced mandatory identity verification for company directors and PSCs in the UK?
options: Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023
Companies Act 2006

testPool.prompt: Which Act supplied the structural template — including the 'reasonable/adequate procedures' defence — for the new failure to prevent fraud offence?
options: Bribery Act 2010
Fraud Act 2006

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the two-of-three thresholds used to define a 'large organisation' for the failure to prevent fraud offence?
options: Annual turnover above £36 million
Balance sheet total above £18 million
More than 250 employees
The organisation is listed on a recognised stock exchange
testPool.trapExplanation: Listing status is not one of the thresholds at all. The test is meeting at least two of: turnover above £36 million, balance sheet total above £18 million, and more than 250 employees — a private, unlisted company meeting two of these thresholds is caught just as much as a listed one.

testPool.prompt: Why does the failure to prevent fraud offence not require proof that a director personally knew about the fraud?
options: Because it deliberately follows the 'failure to prevent' model, which attaches liability to inadequate organisational systems rather than requiring a guilty senior mind
Because all fraud offences in English law have always dispensed with any mental element
Because the offence only applies to fraud committed by directors themselves
testPool.trapExplanation: Fraud offences generally do require a mental element for the individual who commits the underlying fraud — what's distinctive here is that the organisation's liability doesn't require a senior individual's guilty mind to be attributed to it, unlike the older identification doctrine. The offence also applies to fraud by any associated person, not only directors.

testPool.prompt: In this extract, highlight the sentence stating the organisation's defence to the failure to prevent fraud offence.
testPool.passage: A relevant body is guilty of an offence where an associated person commits a specified fraud offence intending to benefit the relevant body. It is a defence for the relevant body to show that, at the time of the offence, it had in place such prevention procedures as it was reasonable in all the circumstances to expect, or that it was not reasonable to expect it to have any such procedures. The defence is assessed by reference to guidance on reasonable procedures, not a fixed checklist.
testPool.ratioSentence: It is a defence for the relevant body to show that, at the time of the offence, it had in place such prevention procedures as it was reasonable in all the circumstances to expect, or that it was not reasonable to expect it to have any such procedures.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that determines whether this company is a 'large organisation' for the failure to prevent fraud offence.
testPool.scenarioText: The company operates in the construction sector and has existed for fifteen years. It has 310 employees, an annual turnover of £22 million, and a balance sheet total of £15 million. Its head office is in Manchester.
testPool.explanation: The company meets the employee threshold (more than 250) even though its turnover and balance sheet total fall below the other two thresholds. Meeting any two of the three thresholds is enough, so if it can be shown to meet one more — for instance, if this year's figures push turnover or the balance sheet over the line — it would qualify; on these facts alone, only the employee threshold is clearly met, so this is the fact to check first.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that shows Companies House's enhanced powers, rather than identity verification, are the relevant pillar of ECCTA.
testPool.scenarioText: A company files a confirmation statement listing a PSC whose verified identity details do not match the details previously submitted. The registrar queries the discrepancy and rejects the filing pending clarification. The company's shareholders are frustrated by the delay.
tappableSpans: verified identity details do not match
registrar queries the discrepancy and rejects the filing
shareholders are frustrated by the delay
testPool.correctSpan: registrar queries the discrepancy and rejects the filing
testPool.explanation: The act of querying and rejecting the filing is the registrar exercising its new enhanced powers under Part 1 of ECCTA — identity verification supplied the underlying data that revealed the discrepancy, but the query-and-reject step itself is the separate, second pillar in action.

testPool.prompt: A large organisation discovers that a rogue senior manager committed fraud that benefited only themselves personally, with no intention to benefit the organisation at all, and against its clear internal policies. Does the failure to prevent fraud offence apply?
options: No — the offence requires the associated person to have intended to benefit the relevant body (or a person it provides services to), which is absent here
Yes — any fraud by any employee of a large organisation automatically triggers the offence
Yes, but only if the organisation had no fraud prevention procedures at all
testPool.explanation: The offence requires an intention to benefit the relevant body (or, in some cases, a client the associated person serves on its behalf). Fraud committed purely for personal gain, with no intended benefit to the organisation, falls outside the offence, whatever the organisation's size or procedures.

testPool.prompt: An existing director, appointed well before 18 November 2025, has not yet completed identity verification but the transition window has not yet closed. Is their appointment currently invalid?
options: No — existing directors have a transition window to complete verification before non-verification affects their status
Yes — every unverified director has been automatically removed from the register
Yes, but only if they are also a PSC
testPool.explanation: The phased approach gives existing directors and PSCs a transition window to verify, distinct from the immediate requirement for new appointments from 18 November 2025. Only once that window closes without verification does the harder consequence (invalid status, filing rejection) bite.

testPool.prompt: A large engineering firm meeting the size thresholds has a written fraud prevention policy, but it has not been updated in six years, no staff training has been delivered on it, and a regional manager exploits an obvious gap in expense-approval controls to submit fraudulent invoices benefiting the firm's reported profits. Analyse whether the firm is likely to have a defence to the failure to prevent fraud offence.
factsToOrder: The firm meets the size thresholds for a 'large organisation'
A written fraud prevention policy exists but has not been updated in six years
No staff training has been delivered on the policy
A regional manager exploits a known control gap
The fraud benefits the firm's reported profits

Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the firm has a defence to the failure to prevent fraud offence under s 199/Sch 12 ECCTA 2023.
modelAnswer.rule: The offence is made out where an associated person commits a specified fraud offence intending to benefit the relevant body, subject to a defence that the organisation had reasonable fraud prevention procedures in place, assessed by reference to guidance on matters such as risk assessment, proportionate policies, training and monitoring — modelled on the Bribery Act 2010 s 7 'adequate procedures' defence.
modelAnswer.application: The elements of the offence are met: the regional manager, an associated person, committed fraud intending to benefit the firm's reported profits, and the firm meets the size thresholds. On the defence, an outdated policy with no staff training and a known, unaddressed control gap strongly suggests the firm's procedures were not reasonable in all the circumstances — a written policy alone is unlikely to satisfy the defence without genuine implementation, updating and monitoring.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The firm is likely to be found guilty, since its fraud prevention procedures, though nominally in place, appear inadequate in substance; a court would look for genuine, current and monitored controls rather than a stale document.

testPool.prompt: State the date the failure to prevent fraud offence came into force.
Put these ECCTA-related developments in chronological order.
items: The failure to prevent fraud offence comes into force (1 September 2025)
Identity verification begins rolling out for new appointments and incorporations (18 November 2025)
The transition window for existing directors and PSCs to verify continues to run

testPool.prompt: Under the registrar's new statutory objectives, which of these is a power the registrar gained specifically to support the accuracy objective?
options: The power to query information delivered to it and require further evidence before accepting a filing
The power to set corporation tax rates
The power to strike off any company without any statutory process at all
testPool.explanation: Querying information and requiring further evidence is a direct ECCTA power supporting the registrar's accuracy and anti-fraud objectives. Tax-setting is outside the registrar's function entirely, and striking off remains subject to its own statutory process, not an unfettered power.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario best illustrates the identification doctrine's limitation, which the failure to prevent fraud offence was designed to avoid?
testPool.scenarioA: A large company cannot be prosecuted for a junior employee's fraud under the old model because no sufficiently senior individual personally had the guilty knowledge needed to be attributed to the company.
testPool.scenarioB: A large company is prosecuted under the failure to prevent fraud offence after a regional manager's fraud benefiting the company is shown alongside inadequate prevention procedures.
testPool.explanation: A shows the identification doctrine's gap: without a sufficiently senior 'directing mind' personally at fault, the company escaped liability under the older model. B shows the new offence in operation, precisely the outcome the reform was designed to make possible without needing to find a guilty senior individual.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is collapsing the three ECCTA pillars — identity verification, Companies House's powers, and failure to prevent fraud — into one undifferentiated reform, or assuming rollout dates and deadlines are more settled than they are. Check which pillar a question is actually testing, and treat exact transition dates as things to verify against current guidance, not fixed facts to memorise permanently.
